1. Validate the current bill: confirm meter reads imply 1,191 kWh (50,037 − 48,846), line items sum to $218.60 ($18.79 + $41.42 + $158.39), and the change versus last month is +$73.49 ($218.60 − $145.11); treat any arithmetic mismatch as a suspected billing error.

2. Map both billing periods to the AEP Ohio tariffs by date: last month (2026-05-25 to 2026-06-23) and current (2026-06-23 to 2026-07-28) both fall entirely under the post-2026-04-10 tariff (fixed $18.788; tier-1 variable $0.0347738 + $0.13299 = $0.1677638/kWh for the first 2,000 kWh), so there is no rate change and price_usd = 0.

3. Compute days_usd from the longer period: 35 days versus 29 days (+6 days); value the extra days at last month's average daily bill ($145.11 ÷ 29 ≈ $5.00/day), giving roughly +$30.02 (or assign all length-related consumption to usage instead, as long as the method is consistent).

4. Estimate weather_usd from NOAA degree days: compare last month (CDD 158 / HDD 6) to current (CDD 430.5 / HDD 0), derive a weather-to-kWh coefficient from the bill history, convert the weather-driven kWh difference to dollars at the effective variable rate, or set weather_usd = 0 if no defensible coefficient can be estimated.

5. Set usage_usd as the residual so price_usd + days_usd + weather_usd + usage_usd equals exactly +$73.49; this captures household usage changes not explained by price, days, or weather.

6. Check for a billing error: model the current period with the tariff (fixed $18.788 + 1,191 kWh × $0.1677638 ≈ $218.60) and last month similarly (≈ $145.11); both match the actual totals within rounding, so billing_error_suspected = false and billing_error_usd = null.

7. Return only the JSON object with keys price_usd, days_usd, weather_usd, usage_usd, billing_error_suspected, and billing_error_usd.
